seo_title: Denied Insurance Claim in Texas? What an Appraiser Can Do
meta_description: Denied insurance claim in Texas? Learn why claims are denied, what to do first, when appraisal can help, and when to call an attorney. Free claim reviews.
h1: Denied Insurance Claim? Here's What an Appraiser Can Do
excerpt: Got a denied insurance claim in Texas? Learn why claims are denied, the first steps to take, when an appraiser can help, and when you need an attorney instead.
key_takeaways: Get the specific denial reason and policy provisions in writing.
Amount and causation disputes may be appraisable; pure coverage denials usually are not.
Independent inspections and line-item estimates are the strongest response to a denial.
If the insurer refuses appraisal or denies coverage outright, consult a Texas attorney.
Texas deadlines, including Chapter 542A's 61-day notice, keep running after a denial.
body_html:
A denied insurance claim is not always the final word. In Texas, start by getting the denial reason in writing, reviewing your policy and documenting the damage independently. If the denial really turns on how much damage occurred or what caused it, rather than whether the policy covers it, an insurance appraiser may help through the policy's appraisal clause.

Opening a denial letter from your insurance company is discouraging, especially after a storm or fire has already turned your life upside down. But many denials rest on incomplete inspections, disputed causation or low damage estimates, not on a clear lack of coverage. This guide explains why claims get denied, what to do first, when an appraiser can help and when you need an attorney instead.

Why are insurance claims denied so often?

Carriers deny or reduce claims for many reasons. Some are legitimate; others are worth challenging. Understanding the stated reason is the first step, because it determines which path makes sense.

Common denial reasonWhat it usually meansCan appraisal help?
"Damage is below your deductible"Carrier's estimate is too low to produce a paymentOften yes; this is an amount-of-loss dispute
"Wear and tear" or "age-related deterioration"Carrier attributes damage to aging, not the stormOften; appraisers may assess causation as part of the amount of loss
"No storm-related damage found"Adjuster did not identify covered damageSometimes, depending on whether coverage itself is disputed
"Cosmetic damage only"Policy has a cosmetic exclusion and carrier applied itPartly; the extent of functional damage may be appraisable, the exclusion is not
Excluded peril (flood, earth movement)Policy does not cover the cause of lossGenerally no; this is a coverage question
Late notice or policy conditionCarrier says you did not meet a policy requirementGenerally no; this is a legal or coverage question

Notice the pattern. When the dispute is about how much damage or what caused it, appraisal may be available. When it is about whether the policy covers the loss at all, it usually is not. Many denied insurance claims fall somewhere in between, so read the letter closely and identify each separate reason the carrier gave.

What should you do first after a claim denial?

  1. Get the denial in writing. Ask the carrier for a letter that states the specific reasons and policy provisions it relied on.
  2. Request the claim file materials you can get, including the adjuster's photos, estimate and any engineering report.
  3. Read your full policy, including declarations, endorsements and the appraisal clause.
  4. Document the damage yourself with date-stamped photos and video. Our claim documentation checklist lists what to gather.
  5. Get an independent inspection from a qualified contractor or roofer who documents storm-related damage specifically.
  6. Mitigate further damage with tarps or drying, and keep receipts.
  7. Track deadlines. Policy limits and Texas law set timelines. Use our Texas claim deadline calculator.
Tip: Respond to the denial in writing, not just by phone. A short letter that lists the evidence you have and asks the carrier to reconsider creates a record and often triggers a reinspection.

What can an insurance appraiser actually do for a denied claim?

An insurance appraiser is appointed under your policy's appraisal clause to help determine the amount of loss. On the policyholder side, the appraiser:

  • Inspects the property thoroughly and documents every damaged component.
  • Writes a detailed, line-item estimate in Xactimate or Symbility, the same platforms carriers use.
  • Analyzes the carrier's estimate and identifies missing scope, low pricing and measurement errors.
  • Presents evidence on causation and extent of damage where appropriate.
  • Negotiates with the carrier's appraiser and, if needed, presents the case to the umpire.

Joseph Dittman, the appraiser behind TX Insurance Appraiser, has spent his career on the policyholder side of Texas property claims, inspecting hail, wind, water and fire losses and writing line-item estimates. On an appraisal assignment, he serves as your appraiser, not as your public adjuster or attorney. For a side-by-side look at the roles, read insurance appraiser vs adjuster.

Can you invoke appraisal after a denied claim?

It depends on why the claim was denied. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), the Texas Supreme Court held that appraisers decide the amount of loss and may assess the cause and extent of damage, but they do not decide coverage or liability. That means:

  • A "below deductible" denial is usually an amount-of-loss dispute and a strong candidate for appraisal.
  • A denial based on wear and tear versus storm damage may be appraisable, because the panel can evaluate causation as part of the amount of loss.
  • A denial based on an excluded peril, late notice or a policy condition is a coverage issue that appraisal generally cannot resolve.

We go deeper in can you invoke appraisal after a denied claim. This is general information, not legal advice.

How does the insurance appraisal process work?

  1. You or the carrier sends a written appraisal demand under the policy.
  2. Each side names a competent, disinterested appraiser within the time the policy allows.
  3. The appraisers choose an umpire, or a court appoints one if they cannot agree.
  4. The appraisers inspect, exchange estimates and try to agree on the amount of loss.
  5. Any items they cannot resolve go to the umpire.
  6. An award signed by two of the three generally sets the amount of loss.

Most residential appraisals resolve in a matter of months, depending on responsiveness and whether an umpire is needed. See how long an insurance appraisal takes for typical timelines.

What if the insurer refuses appraisal?

Carriers sometimes refuse appraisal, often arguing the dispute is about coverage rather than amount. If your policy contains an appraisal clause and the dispute genuinely involves the amount of loss, Texas courts generally enforce valid appraisal demands. A party that refuses can be asked to participate through a court order.

This is where the line between an appraiser and an attorney matters. TX Insurance Appraiser is not a law firm and does not give legal advice. If the carrier refuses appraisal, denies coverage outright, or you suspect unfair claim handling under Chapter 541 of the Texas Insurance Code, speak with a Texas insurance attorney. Remember that Chapter 542A generally requires 61 days' written notice before filing suit on weather-related claims. You can also file a complaint with the Texas Department of Insurance at tdi.texas.gov.

How do you build a strong case after a denial?

  • Photos and video of all damage, with dates, locations and scale.
  • Weather data showing hail, wind or storm activity at your address on the date of loss.
  • Independent inspection reports from qualified contractors or roofers.
  • A line-item estimate that mirrors the carrier's format so differences are clear.
  • Prior condition evidence such as inspection reports or earlier photos showing the property before the loss.
  • 3D documentation. A Matterport 3D scan preserves interior conditions before cleanup or repairs.
  • Every letter and email exchanged with the carrier.

Strong documentation turns a denied insurance claim from your word against the adjuster's into a dispute about evidence. It helps whether you negotiate directly, invoke appraisal or work with an attorney.

Mistakes to avoid after a denied insurance claim

  • Assuming the denial is final and walking away from a valid claim.
  • Making permanent repairs before damage is documented and the carrier has had a chance to reinspect.
  • Relying on phone calls rather than written requests and responses.
  • Missing policy or statutory deadlines while waiting for the carrier to change its mind.
  • Invoking appraisal on a pure coverage denial, where it is unlikely to help.

What about partial denials and underpaid claims?

Many claims are not denied outright. Instead, the carrier pays for part of the damage and denies the rest, such as paying for gutters and screens but not the roof, or paying for one room of water damage but not the adjoining rooms. A partial denial can cost as much as a full one.

Partial denials are often a mix of coverage and amount-of-loss issues. The carrier may accept that a storm occurred but dispute how many slopes were damaged, whether repairs are feasible or what the work costs. Those portions of the dispute are frequently suited to appraisal. Our guide to the signs your insurance claim was underpaid can help you tell whether your settlement is short.

For example, if a carrier pays $4,000 for collateral damage but denies the roof as wear and tear, and your roofer documents functional hail damage on every slope, the roof dispute may be appraisable even though the carrier has called it a denial.

When should you call an insurance appraiser?

Consider contacting an appraiser when:

  • The carrier says damage is below the deductible, but your contractor's estimate is much higher.
  • The denial blames wear and tear, and you have evidence of storm damage.
  • A partial denial pays for some damage but leaves out major components.
  • Reinspections and supplements have not changed the carrier's position.
  • You want an independent opinion on whether appraisal is worth the cost.

faqs.q: Can I dispute a denied insurance claim in Texas?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask for the denial reasons in writing, gather independent evidence, and request reconsideration or a reinspection. If the dispute is about the amount of loss or cause of damage, appraisal may be available. If the carrier denies coverage outright or handles the claim unfairly, a Texas insurance attorney or a TDI complaint may be appropriate.

faqs.q: Is an insurance appraiser the same as an attorney?
faqs.a: No. An insurance appraiser is appointed under the policy's appraisal clause to help determine the amount of loss. An attorney gives legal advice and can file suit over coverage, bad faith or statutory violations. Appraisers cannot decide coverage or give legal advice, so some claims need both professionals at different stages.

faqs.q: What does below deductible mean on a denied claim?
faqs.a: It means the carrier's estimate of covered damage is less than your deductible, so it owes no payment. This is often an amount-of-loss dispute. If your contractor's line-item estimate shows significantly more damage, appraisal may be a way to have an independent panel determine the actual amount of loss.

faqs.q: How long do I have to challenge a denied claim in Texas?
faqs.a: Many Texas policies require lawsuits within two years and one day from when the claim accrues, and weather-related suits generally require 61 days' written notice under Chapter 542A. Appraisal clauses may not set a specific deadline, but waiting can weaken your position. Review your policy and get advice before key dates pass.

faqs.q: Can I file a complaint with the Texas Department of Insurance?
faqs.a: Yes. The Texas Department of Insurance accepts consumer complaints about insurers, including claim handling concerns. A complaint does not decide your claim or force payment, but TDI may contact the carrier and ask for a response. It can be a useful step alongside negotiation, appraisal or legal advice.
